name: Gata Bera Drum
description: The gata bera is the large cylindrical drum of Sri Lanka, slung from the hip and beaten with sticks or open hands at Buddhist perahera processions, temple rites, village festivals and healing ceremonies. Its name comes from the Sinhala word for a pot, and the barrel is traditionally carved from jak or asala wood with heads of cowhide braced by rope and leather thongs, tuned so the deep beat carries over crowds. It is the lead drum of the Kandyan dance tradition, where drummers and dancers train together from boyhood, and it also drives the masked exorcism dances that the Sinhalese perform to pacify the sanni and riri yaksha, the disease demons of the folk tradition. A Sinhalese story holds that the drum's rhythms were first given by a god, and the instrument remains the sound of celebration and of healing alike in the island's ritual life.
source: Sinhalese ritual and festival practice

name: Sanni Yaksha Mask
description: The sanni yaksha mask is a carved and painted wooden face of a Sinhalese disease demon, worn in the exorcism rites that Sri Lankan tradition calls shanthi karma or tovil. There are eighteen principal sanni demons, each named for a particular affliction, such as fever, madness, dropsy or jaundice, and each has its own mask with a distinctive colour, expression and headdress. The finest carving comes from Ambalangoda on the south coast, where the mask carvers cut the traditional kaduru wood and finish it with vegetable and mineral pigments. In the ritual the masked dancer enacts the demon's story to coax it into speech, then frightens or bribes it into leaving the sick body, so the mask is both an artwork and a working instrument of healing. The ceremony is said to recall a plague once healed by a healer at Vaishali, and the sanni masks are still danced today in Sri Lanka.
source: Sinhalese ritual ethnography and mask-carving tradition

name: Ajrak
description: The ajrak is the block-printed shawl of Sindh, stamped in deep indigo and madder red with concentric borders of geometric stars, flowers and trellis patterns, worn over the shoulder and used to cover sacred objects. The name is linked to the Arabic word for blue, and archaeologists point to indigo-dyed and resist-printed cotton found at the Indus valley site of Mohenjo-daro as evidence that such cloth was made in the region thousands of years ago. A single ajrak may pass through some twenty-one stages of washing, printing and dyeing, using wooden blocks carved by hereditary craftsmen and mordants of iron and alum, so the finished shawl carries the redness of the earth and the blue of the river. It is a strong marker of Sindhi identity, draped at weddings, offered to guests and honoured guests, and presented as a mark of respect on formal occasions.
source: Craft history of Sindh and Sindhi cultural practice

name: Sindhi Topi
description: The sindhi topi is the embroidered cylindrical cap of Sindh, worn by men at daily work and at festivals, with a rounded crown and a characteristic arch-shaped cut-out above the forehead edged with stitched mirror work. The caps are made across the province, with centres such as Tharparkar known for fine needlework, and the shape and embroidery vary from town to town so that the topi can show where a wearer comes from. Sindhi tradition pairs the cap with the ajrak shawl, and the two together are treated as a badge of the province's culture; Sindhi Cultural Day is marked by wearing both. A widely repeated saying holds that the topi carries the honour and pride of the man who wears it, so that knocking it from his head is a grave insult, and the cap is a fixture of Sindhi weddings, political gatherings and everyday dress.
source: Sindhi cultural tradition

name: Butterfly Jigha
description: The butterfly jigha is a jewel-set turban ornament of Mughal court fashion, shaped as a butterfly with wings that tremble on a spring as the wearer moves, pinned to the front of the turban by princes, nobles and high officials. Such ornaments are shown in Mughal miniature painting and in later court portraiture of the Deccan and the regions that became Pakistan, where the jigha, sarpesh and other turban jewels marked rank and the favour of the ruler. Surviving examples worked in gold and enamel with rubies, emeralds and pearls sometimes include a socket for a heron or egret plume that rose above the turban, a feature historically restricted to the royal family and those granted the privilege. The butterfly form with its quivering spring is one of the most recognisable types in museum collections, prized for the delicate chasing and stone-setting of the court jewellers.
source: Museum holdings (e.g. V&A O73036) and Mughal painting

name: Naqqara Drum
description: The naqqara is a pair of kettledrums, usually of copper with goatskin heads, beaten with two sticks and carried before rulers or sounded from gate towers to announce arrivals, processions and festival days. The instrument came into South Asia with the Indo-Islamic courts, where paired kettledrums were part of royal ceremonial music, and it remains in use at shrines and at processions across Pakistan and the wider Muslim world. In the Punjab and Sindh the deep paired notes of the naqqara mark the high moments of a gathering, and the drum is still played at the doors of shrines and at the head of festival processions, where its sound is said to carry the blessing of the occasion through the crowd. Naqqara bands of several drums of different sizes are also a feature of military and civic celebration in the region.
maker: drum makers of the Punjab and Sindh
source: Indo-Islamic court and shrine musical tradition

name: Karahi
description: The karahi is the deep rounded pan of Pakistan, forged from cast iron or pressed steel, with two handles and steep sides, set over an open flame to cook the spiced stew that shares its name. The name of the vessel has passed to the dish itself, and a karahi of lamb, chicken or vegetables cooked with tomato, green chilli and ginger is one of the most familiar foods of Pakistani homes, roadside dhabas and bazaars, served hot straight from the pan with fresh naan. Because the karahi sits directly on the fire, the oil and spices fry hard before liquid is added, giving the gravy its characteristic rich colour and edge. It is the daily cooking vessel of many households and the centre of festive and communal meals, and iron karahis are prized for seasoning with use, so that old pans are handed down within families.
source: Pakistani domestic culinary tradition

name: Rilli Quilt
description: The rilli quilt is the patchwork bedding of Sindh, sewn by women from scraps and recycled cotton cloth cut into triangles, diamonds, squares and zigzag bands and joined in bright, ordered compositions. The craft is passed from mother to daughter, and the same word covers quilts made by applique, patchwork or embroidery, often combining several techniques in one cover. A rilli is laid over winter bedding or spread on the floor for guests, and quilts are made ahead of a wedding as part of the bride's trousseau, so a well-made rilli carries the reputation of the maker's skill and the household's fortunes. The patterns are traditional but not fixed, and women reuse older quilts and garment cloth so that each piece carries a history of the family's cloth and needlework across the generations of rural Sindh.
source: Sindhi folk textile tradition

name: Khukuri
description: The khukuri is the curved blade of the Nepali Gurkha tradition, broad and heavy near the tip, tapering to the hilt, and used for cutting wood, clearing brush, daily chores and ceremonial display. The name is spelled kukri in British usage, and the blade is forged by Nepali kamis, the metal-working caste, who shape it at a charcoal forge and temper the cutting edge while leaving the spine soft enough to absorb shock. It is carried in a leather scabbard together with two smaller knives, the karda for fine work and the chakmak for sharpening, and the distinctive notch at the blade's base is a mark of the traditional shape. A well-known folk saying holds that once the khukuri is drawn it must taste blood before being sheathed again, a custom linked to its history as a weapon of war and to the rituals of the Gurkha regiments.
source: Nepali folk custom and Gurkha regimental tradition

name: Mukut Crown
description: The mukut is the jewel-set crown of the royal traditions of Nepal, worn by the Malla kings of the Kathmandu valley and later the Shah kings at state and religious ceremonies, and linked by tradition to the goddess Taleju, protector of the ruling dynasties. The crowns are worked in gold and silver with gemstones, pearls and brocade by the Newar goldsmiths of Kathmandu, and the king's crown was held to draw its right to rule from the favour of Taleju, whose temples stood beside the royal palaces. The living goddess tradition also places a crown on the young Kumari during festivals, echoing the belief that divine favour descends on the wearer. Royal regalia of this kind survives in the museums of Kathmandu and in the courts' surviving records, and the mukut remains a powerful image of Nepali kingship.
source: Newar court tradition and museum regalia holdings

name: Thangka
description: The thangka is the painted or embroidered scroll image of Tibetan Buddhism, hung in monasteries, homes and shrines across the Himalayan world and framed in a silk brocade border. The painter first lays out a precise iconometric grid on cotton or silk, then works with mineral pigments and gold in the traditional palettes of the Newar and monastic painters, finishing with an outline in black and the consecration of the image. The subjects are buddhas, bodhisattvas, fierce protectors, mandalas and scenes of the lives of the saints, and each figure must follow strict proportions and attributes so the painting can serve as an aid to meditation and as a support for the deity's presence. A thangka is treated with respect, hung in a clean high place, and often blessed, and the form has been painted continuously for centuries from the monasteries of Nepal and Tibet.
material: cotton or silk, mineral pigments, gold
source: Himalayan Buddhist painting tradition

name: Singing Bowl
description: The singing bowl is a metal bowl of the Himalayan Buddhist world that produces a long, sustained tone when its rim is rubbed with a wooden striker or struck, and it is used in offerings, meditation and the opening and closing of ceremonies. The bowls are cast in bronze and brass bell-metal alloys, often in the workshops of the Kathmandu valley, and many carry embossed decoration or an incised invocation such as the six-syllable mantra Om Mani Padme Hum. Their use in ritual is old, though the precise history is uncertain, and the bowls became widely known outside the Himalayas only from the late twentieth century, when the trade through Patan and Thamel grew and the sound was adopted in meditation circles. Monks and lay people alike treat the ringing as an offering to the deities and a way of clearing and focusing the mind.
source: Himalayan ritual practice and craft tradition

name: Mani Wall
description: The mani wall is a long, low wall of carved stone raised beside mountain paths, passes and villages across the Himalayan world, its blocks inscribed with the six-syllable mantra Om Mani Padme Hum and set in rows under a capping course of stones. The name comes from the first syllable of the mantra, which is the prayer of the bodhisattva of compassion Avalokiteshvara, and the walls are treated as sacred, so that travellers keep them on their right and walk past them clockwise, the direction of ritual circumambulation. Passing pilgrims and travellers add their own stones, carved or plain, so the wall grows as a living offering along the route, and the carved stones are believed to carry blessing to everyone who walks by, whether or not they can read the letters. Long chains of mani walls line the pilgrim roads of Nepal, Ladakh and the approaches to Mount Kailash.
source: Himalayan Buddhist pilgrimage practice

name: Sherpa Pangden
description: The sherpa pangden is the striped front apron woven and worn by Sherpa married women over their chuba, the strip of red, white and black stripes marking the wearer's married status and adulthood. The aprons are woven on backstrap looms from sheep's and yak's wool, and the narrow stripes and their colours follow family and regional convention, so that the pangden is a badge of household and of womanhood as much as a piece of dress. The custom is hundreds of years old and is also found among related Himalayan peoples and in Tibetan regions, where similar striped aprons are made. A girl receives her pangden as she comes of age and is expected to wear it in daily life and at festivals, and the making of the aprons remains a home craft of Sherpa women weavers in the valleys below the Everest massif.
source: Sherpa weaving and dress ethnography (Dolma Sherpa)

name: Dorje
description: The dorje is the ritual thunderbolt of Bhutanese and Tibetan Buddhism, a bronze or gilt sceptre with a central grip and prongs that curve inward at each end, held in monastic hand rituals and placed on altars. The word is the Tibetan translation of the Sanskrit vajra, and it means lord of stones, hard as diamond and indestructible as the thunderbolt; the five prongs of the common form stand for the five Dhyani Buddhas and their wisdoms. In the older Hindu and Buddhist myth the vajra was the thunder-weapon of the god Indra, and in Himalayan ritual the dorje is paired with the hand bell, held in the right hand while the bell sounds in the left. Monks raise the dorje through ceremonies and empowerments, where it represents the unbreakable method of enlightenment that the practitioner cultivates.
source: Bhutanese monastic ritual tradition

name: Drilbu Bell
description: The drilbu is the ritual hand bell of Himalayan Buddhism, cast in a bell-metal alloy so that it rings a long, clear note, and struck or rung during ceremonies as the companion of the dorje sceptre. The bell is held in the left hand while the dorje is held in the right, and the two together are used in most monastic rituals of the Tibetan schools. The handle of the drilbu is cast as the face of a deity, most often the goddess Prajnaparamita, the embodiment of wisdom, whose head forms the knob above a vajra finial. The sound of the bell is used to summon the attention of the practitioner and the deities, to mark the turning points of a rite, and to fill the space of the ritual, and its tone is said to carry the compassion and clarity that the ceremony invokes.
source: Bhutanese monastic ritual tradition

name: Bhutanese Festival Mask
description: The Bhutanese festival mask is a carved and painted wooden face worn by dancers in the cham dances of Bhutanese monasteries, taking the forms of fierce deities, animals, black-hatted dancers and the skeleton guardians of the faith. The tradition of cham is said to have been brought to the Himalayan world by the teacher Padmasambhava, and the dances are performed in the courtyards of the dzongs during the yearly tsechu festivals, when onlookers gather to see the masked dancers turn in slow circles to drum and cymbal. Each mask follows strict iconographic rules, and the identities of the dancers are kept within the monasteries, while the lay people watch and are held to receive blessing and protection from the performance. The festival masks are made by Bhutanese carvers, painted with mineral colours, and are among the most recognisable art forms of the kingdom.
source: Bhutanese monastic dance (cham) tradition

name: Nakshi Kantha
description: The nakshi kantha is the embroidered quilt of Bengal, sewn by village women from stacked layers of old saris and dhotis and covered with running stitch in patterns of flowers, birds, animals, boats and scenes of daily life. The name comes from the fine nakshi stitching, and the needlework is built up by hand so that the whole surface becomes a picture, with borders, corner motifs and a central lotus or mandala medallion. A kantha made for a bride is a gift of love and skill, and the making of kanthas is passed between mothers, daughters and granddaughters, each woman adding motifs from memory and imagination. The craft is practised across Bangladesh and West Bengal, and finished quilts are used as bedding, wraps and covers, treasured as much for the maker's hand as for their warmth.
source: Bengali folk textile tradition

name: Dhakai Jamdani
description: The dhakai jamdani is the handwoven muslin of the Dhaka region, patterned with fine floral, geometric and figural motifs that are worked into the cloth itself on the loom, rather than printed or embroidered after weaving. The weaver picks out each motif with extra weft threads, often of silver or gold, using a technique of supplementary weft float work, so that the pattern appears woven through the sheer, fine-count cotton. The craft was patronised by the Mughal courts and has been practised for centuries along the banks of the rivers around Dhaka and Narayanganj, and it was inscribed by UNESCO on the list of intangible cultural heritage in 2013. Jamdani saris remain prized ceremonial dress for weddings and festivals across Bengal and beyond.
source: UNESCO intangible heritage listing and craft history

name: Ghot Pot
description: The ghot is the pot placed before the bride and groom in the ashirbad blessing of Bengali Hindu weddings, a brass or clay vessel filled with paddy, durba grass and other auspicious items, with a red-and-white thread tied around its mouth. The word ghot covers the pot itself and its role in the blessing, and the pot is kept in the wedding space while the elders speak their good wishes over the couple. The paddy stands for grain and fertility, the durba grass for growth and prosperity, and the ghats are prepared by the women of the two families as part of the wedding's household ritual. The pot is a small, everyday object carrying a large ceremonial meaning, and the same kind of vessel appears in other Hindu rites of the region as a seat for the divine presence.
source: Bengali Hindu wedding custom (Antrocom marriage-customs study)

name: Ektara
description: The ektara is the one-stringed lute of rural Bengal, made from a gourd or a bamboo tube with a skin face and a single steel string that is plucked and struck to produce a thin, continuous drone. It is the instrument of the wandering Baul singers of Bengal, who carry the ektara with their other small instruments and sing songs of the divine within the human body, of love and of the inner search, in an oral tradition that is not written down. The Bauls move from village to village, and the drone of the ektara sets the rhythm and pitch for the song, sometimes with a gopichand drum in the other hand. The instrument is simple to make and to carry, and its name means one string, so that the whole music of the sect is often summed up in the single note it produces.
source: Baul oral tradition of Bengal

name: Khyber Knife
description: The khyber knife is the long, straight-backed belt knife of the frontier regions of Afghanistan and the border country of the Khyber Pass, with a wide spine, a single cutting edge and a simple handle of horn, bone or wood. It is worn at the belt and used for cutting, skinning and defence, and the name comes from the pass that links the Afghan highlands with the plains, a corridor of trade and conflict for centuries. Frontier bladesmiths forged the knives for daily work and for display, and the handles of older examples are often incised or decorated, showing the owner's pride in the weapon. The khyber knife appears in the material culture of the borderlands and in ethnographic collections of frontier weaponry, a practical tool that also served as a mark of the bearer.
material: steel, horn or bone handle, leather
source: Ethnographic collections of frontier weaponry

name: Herati Carpet
description: The herati carpet is a hand-knotted wool carpet of the Herat region of western Afghanistan, woven with repeating medallion, star and floral patterns that have been exported from the city for centuries. The trade flourished under the Timurid court, when Herat was a centre of craft and patronage, and the rug's patterns are still carried by weaving families who pass the designs from one generation to the next. The name herati is also attached in the rug trade to a pattern with a central diamond, hooked leaves and corner motifs, and the same terms cause lasting confusion with the rugs of Heriz in north-west Iran, which are distinct carpets from a different region. Afghan herati rugs are made of wool on cotton warps, often with the reds and blues of madder and indigo dyes, and are laid as household and prayer carpets.
source: Carpet history of the Herat weaving region

name: Kuchi Jewelry
description: The kuchi jewelry is the heavy silver ornament of the Kuchi, the nomadic herding people of Afghanistan, who carry their wealth on their persons in the form of large necklaces, headpieces, earrings, bracelets and belt buckles. The pieces are made of silver, often with added amber, carnelian, turquoise and glass beads, and the forms echo ancient styles of Central Asia, with coin-rimmed discs, stamped patterns and chains that jingle as the wearer moves. For a nomadic family, jewelry is a portable bank, and for a bride the dowry ornaments show the status and resources of the two families. Kuchi jewelry is made by silversmiths who work for the nomad trade, and older pieces are collected and reused, so the ornaments carry the history of generations of wandering life across the Afghan plains.
source: Ethnographic documentation of Kuchi material culture

name: Rubab
description: The rubab is the short-necked plucked lute of Afghanistan, carved from a single block of mulberry wood with a belly of animal skin and three main melody strings played with a wooden plectrum. Two or three drone strings and up to a dozen sympathetic strings lie under the playing strings, giving the instrument its deep, ringing sound, and Afghan musicians call it the lion of instruments. It is the lead instrument of the classical music of Kabul and is also played in Pashto folk song and in the Sufi music of the region, and its repertoire runs from court compositions to the songs of the valleys. The rubab is made by instrument makers of Kabul who select the mulberry wood for its sound, and the instrument is taught within families of musicians, passed down through generations.
material: mulberry wood, animal skin, nylon and steel strings
source: Afghan classical music tradition

name: Didgeridoo
description: The didgeridoo is the long wooden trumpet of the Aboriginal peoples of northern Australia, made from a eucalyptus limb whose core has been hollowed by termites, cut, cleaned and fitted with a beeswax mouthpiece. The player vibrates the lips to produce a deep, continuous drone, often with circular breathing so the note never stops, and skilled players add vocal calls and rhythmic syllables over the drone. It accompanies ceremony, song and dance, and in the traditions of northern Australia its sound is connected to the great ancestral beings, including the Rainbow Serpent of the creation stories, who is said to have given the music of the Dreaming. The word didgeridoo is a European coinage from the early twentieth century, while the instrument's own names include yidaki and magaru, and it has spread far beyond Australia as a musical instrument in the decades since.
source: Ethnomusicological and ethnographic scholarship on Aboriginal music

name: Boomerang
description: The boomerang is the curved throwing stick of the Aboriginal peoples of Australia, carved from hardwood and used for hunting, fighting, digging and ceremony. Returning boomerangs are shaped with a twist across the wings so that they curve in flight and come back to the thrower, while heavier non-returning forms are hurled flat and low to strike game or an enemy, and the same shapes were used as clapsticks, digging tools and fire-sticks. The weapons are sometimes engraved or painted with the designs of the maker's clan. The returning boomerang is one of the oldest known engineered tools and was taken up worldwide as a sport object, while in Australia the boomerang remains an emblem of Aboriginal skill and appears in Dreaming stories and modern cultural display.
source: Archaeological and ethnographic studies of Aboriginal technology

name: Coolamon
description: The coolamon is the carved wooden carrying dish of the Aboriginal peoples of Australia, shaped from the root growth of eucalyptus trees or cut from bark, and used to hold water, food, seeds, fire and babies. A single piece of wood is gouged and shaped so that the dish has a curved bottom, and it is carried on the head, in the hand or under the arm, with smaller coolamons made as cradles for infants and larger ones used for grinding seeds and winnowing grain. The dish is a working tool of daily life, used especially by women in food gathering, and it can be painted with the clan designs of the maker. In the desert and riverine regions the coolamon remains a practical and ceremonial vessel, and examples are held in museum collections of Aboriginal material culture.
maker: Aboriginal craftsmen of the riverine and desert peoples
source: Museum and ethnographic records of Aboriginal material culture

name: Woomera
description: The woomera is the spear-throwing lever of the Aboriginal peoples of Australia, a wooden handle with a peg or socket at one end that lengthens the thrower's arm and hurls a spear with far greater force and distance than the arm alone. It is shaped from a flat or curved branch with stone tools, and the peg is fixed with resin, and in the central and western regions it was the standard hunting and fighting weapon, with the same tool doubling as a dish, a digging stick or a fire-maker. The woomera was used across most of the continent, though it was unknown in Tasmania, and in initiation it may be engraved with the designs of the clan and treated with respect. The name entered English from the Dharug language of the Sydney region, and the tool is also known by the name miru in some areas.
maker: Aboriginal craftsmen of central and western Australia
source: Ethnographic records of Aboriginal hunting technology

name: Tjurunga
description: The tjurunga is the sacred board or stone of the Arrernte and other central Australian peoples, engraved with the patterns of the Dreaming and treated as the physical body of an ancestral being. The boards are kept in secret storehouses and brought out for initiation and ceremony, and a tjurunga is handed down as a bond between the living, the land and the ancestral beings, its power bound to the pattern carved on its surface. The name is also spelled churinga, and the classic accounts were written by Spencer and Gillen from the Alice Springs region. Tjurunga are restricted objects of the men's law, and their designs and ceremonies are not shown to the uninitiated or to women, so the published records describe the boards only in general terms and with respect for the secrecy that still surrounds them.
maker: Ancestral law keepers of the Arrernte
source: Spencer and Gillen ethnographic records; Arrernte tradition

name: Clapsticks
description: The clapsticks are the paired hardwood percussion sticks of the Aboriginal peoples of Australia, struck together by singers and dancers to mark the rhythm of ceremony and song. In Arnhem Land they are known as bilma, and they are often painted or engraved with the designs of the clan, with the length and tone of each pair chosen by the songman. The sticks accompany the didgeridoo and the singing in corroboree and ceremony, and each song owns a particular beat that encodes the Dreaming story it carries, so the rhythm is part of the knowledge held by the singers. Clapsticks are simple in form but exact in use, and they are also played by hand-clapping groups where no wood is at hand, in the musical traditions of the north and the centre of Australia.
maker: Aboriginal craftsmen of Arnhem Land and the north
source: Ethnomusicological studies of Aboriginal performance

name: Bullroarer
description: The bullroarer is an oval wooden slat whirled on the end of a cord to produce a low, roaring hum, used by the Aboriginal peoples of Australia in initiation and ceremony. As the slat spins, it cuts the air and the pitch rises and falls with the speed of the whirling, and the sound can carry across a surprising distance. In south-eastern Australia the voice of the bullroarer is sometimes said to be the voice of the ancestor Daramulum, and in many traditions the instrument is kept for the men's law, so that women and children are not shown it. The bullroarer is found in many parts of the world, but in Australia it is bound to the initiation grounds, where its humming warns of the sacred ceremonies taking place and draws the attention of the ancestors to the land.
source: Ethnographic accounts of Aboriginal initiation rites

name: Message Stick
description: The message stick is a carved piece of wood sent between Aboriginal groups to carry news and to prove the authority of the messenger who carries it. The marks cut and painted on the surface record something of the message, the sender's clan and the places or groups concerned, and the stick is accepted as a sign that the bearer speaks with the consent of the people who sent them. The marks are not writing in the modern sense, but they carry meaning within the system of the sender and receiver, and the practice of carrying such sticks is recorded from many parts of Australia. The messenger is greeted with formal welcome when the stick is presented, and the stick itself is often destroyed or returned once the message has been delivered and answered.
source: Colonial ethnographic records; Aboriginal oral tradition

name: Mere Pounamu
description: The mere pounamu is the short, broad-bladed club of the Maori, carved from pounamu, the greenstone of New Zealand, and regarded as a chiefly weapon and a great heirloom. The blade is leaf-shaped and polished, straight-edged and thicker along its length, and the rounded grip is pierced for a wrist cord, so that the club swings with a stroke of the forearm. Named meres were handed down through the generations, and the mana of the weapon passed from hand to hand, with the saying that a chief was lifted by receiving such a weapon. Because pounamu comes from the rivers and mountains of the South Island, the meres of the northern tribes were carried along the trade routes, and the blades were so greatly valued that they were not allowed to touch the ground.
maker: Māori carvers of the South Island pounamu sources
source: Ethnographic scholarship on Māori weaponry and taonga

name: Hei Tiki
description: The hei tiki is the carved greenstone pendant worn at the neck by the Maori, representing a human figure with the head tilted to one side, often with the tongue pointing from the mouth. It is made from pounamu, the nephrite jade of the South Island, and carved with stone drills and abrasive cords in the time before metal tools. The hei tiki is a taonga passed down within families, worn by men and women, and the older a pendant is, the more it is valued, for each one is believed to carry the presence and mana of the ancestors who wore it before. New pendants are given as gifts to mark births, weddings and farewells, and the form appears in Maori tradition in the story of the origin of the tiki, which tells how the first human figure was shaped.
maker: Māori carvers of the greenstone trade routes
source: Ethnographic scholarship on Māori adornment and taonga

name: Tewhatewha
description: The tewhatewha is the long-handled fighting staff of the Maori, a wooden weapon with a flat, axe-like blade at one end and a shaped base, often hung with a bunch of feathers or dog hair at the bottom of the handle. It was swung in sweeping strokes and could be thrust or thrown, and the feathers at the base were used in training and in challenge, flicking and flashing to distract the opponent or to call out a warrior before a duel. The weapon was also carried in war dances and chiefly display as a mark of martial skill, and its handling was taught within the whare-taua, the house of war. The tewhatewha is carved from hardwood or whalebone, and named examples are recorded in the accounts of early European observers of Maori warfare.
source: Ethnographic accounts of Māori weaponry

name: Toki Poutangata
description: The toki poutangata is the ceremonial adze of the Maori, fitted with a blade of pounamu or basalt lashed to a carved wooden handle and hung with a plait of fibre and feathers. Unlike the working adze, the toki poutangata was not used for daily woodwork but was carried before a rangatira and raised in speeches as a badge of chiefly authority, and the finest blades were treasured heirlooms passed down through the great lineages. The name means the adze of the great chief, and the object appears in the ceremonial life of the marae, where the taking up of a toki could mark the acceptance of leadership or the settlement of a dispute. The greenstone blades were cut and ground over long months, so the finished toki carried the labour and skill of its maker as well as the mana of its owner.
material: pounamu or basalt blade, carved wood, fibre
maker: Māori carvers of the adze tradition
source: Ethnographic scholarship on Māori ceremonial objects

name: Kākahu (Māori Cloak)
description: The kakahu is the woven cloak of the Maori, made from the muka fibre of the flax plant and covered with the down, feathers and tags of native birds, and worn as a cloak of rank and prestige. The weaver prepares the flax fibre, spins and dyes it, and weaves the body of the cloak on a small loom, then decorates it with feathers of kiwi, kaka, huia and other birds, or with tags of dog skin and fibre. The finest cloaks, such as the kahu kiwi, were made over months and were worn by chiefs on great occasions, and each cloak carries its own name and history. The black-feathered korowai with hanging tags is among the best-known forms, and kakahu are still woven today and worn at hui and ceremonies, treasured as taonga of the iwi that own them.
source: Ethnographic scholarship on Māori weaving and taonga

name: Kete (Māori Basket)
description: The kete is the woven basket of the Maori, plaited from the strips of the harakeke flax plant and used to carry food, tools, feathers and other goods in daily life. Plain kete are made quickly for carrying, while the patterned kete whakairo is woven with a coloured design and given as a mark of respect. In Maori tradition the three kete of knowledge were brought down from the heavens by the god Tane, who returned with the basket of ritual knowledge, the basket of ancestral knowledge and the basket of practical knowledge, and so established learning among humankind. The kete is therefore both an everyday object and a powerful image of knowledge itself, and the phrase to hand over a kete of knowledge means to teach. Kete are still woven today in the traditional materials and patterns.
source: Māori oral tradition; ethnographic records of weaving

name: Waka Taua (Māori War Canoe)
description: The waka taua is the Maori war canoe, a long carved vessel that carried war parties on raids and conveyed chiefs in ceremony, often paddled by forty or more warriors. It was built from a single totara trunk, with the hull hollowed and shaped by adze, and fitted with carved prow and stern posts, a raised wash-strake and lashings of fibre; the prow commonly carried the carved figure of a taniwha, the guardian water spirit of Maori tradition. The launching and naming of a waka taua were accompanied by ritual and karakia, and the canoe itself was a symbol of tribal mana, so that a great waka bore the name of its tribe and its ancestors. When a war party paddled out, the crew performed haka and chanted in time with the strokes, and the waka was both a transport of war and a work of carved art.
source: Ethnographic accounts of Māori naval technology
